title: Mountains Beyond Mountains: The Quest of Dr. Paul Farmer, a Man Who Would Cure the World
author: Tracy Kidder
target_audience: Readers interested in biographies of humanitarian figures
Those concerned with global health and poverty
Advocates and workers in public health and social change
General readers seeking stories of inspiration and social justice
core_themes: Social justice and the quest to eradicate disease
Sacrifice and perseverance in humanitarian work
primary_purpose: To chronicle the life and work of Dr. Paul Farmer as an exemplar of compassionate, tireless medical activism, and to examine the complexities and challenges of providing quality health care to the world's poorest communities.

structure_format.narrative_style: Immersive narrative nonfiction, blending reportage, biographical storytelling, and investigative journalism
structure_format.organization: Chronological with thematic focus, interwoven with Kidder's personal observations
features: Descriptions of global locations (Haiti, Peru, Russia, US)
Reflection on ethics, medicine, and activism

key_concepts_lessons: Healthcare is a human right, regardless of geography or income.
Personal passion and conviction can drive significant global change.
Addressing poverty is inseparable from improving health outcomes.
Individual actions matter, but long-term change requires working within and against systemic barriers.
Working with, and listening to, local communities is essential for effective public health interventions.
notable_features: In-depth portrayal of a complex humanitarian figure
Rich depiction of cultures and settings affected by poverty and disease
Focus on Partners In Health and its model of community-based care
Integration of philosophical discussions about justice and medicine
cultural_historical_context: Written against the backdrop of late 20th and early 21st-century global health crises (e.g., TB, HIV/AIDS) and the rise of underdog nonprofit organizations challenging international health paradigms. Reflects growing public awareness of global inequality post-Cold War.
reception_impact: Critically acclaimed for humanizing Paul Farmer and the global health movement
Inspired many healthcare professionals, students, and activists to focus on social determinants of health
Raised mainstream awareness about multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and healthcare inequality
Some critics argue the portrait is admiring but not deeply critical of Farmer’s methods
comparable_titles: The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down by Anne Fadiman
The Emperor of All Maladies by Siddhartha Mukherjee
Cutting for Stone by Abraham Verghese (fiction inspired by similar themes)
